analysis.one_liner: Slashes capital gains taxes, indexes investment gains for inflation, and repeals the federal estate tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 1998 with a single cosponsor, the bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the top tax rate on long-term investment gains to 14% (7% for income that would otherwise be taxed in the lowest brackets) and set a 14% rate for corporate capital gains. It would adjust the purchase price of stock and business property for inflation before calculating taxable gains, and it would eliminate the federal estate tax, gift tax, and tax on generation-skipping transfers for transfers made after enactment. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors holding appreciated stock and business property, heirs inheriting large estates, and corporations with capital gains. Because capital gains and taxable estates are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the benefits would flow overwhelmingly to high-income families. Retirement savers holding stock through mutual funds would get a smaller indirect benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, corporations, and heirs of large estates

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current maximum capital gains structure with a 14% rate on net capital gain above the amount taxed at rates below 28%, and 7% on the portion that falls in that lower band, effective for tax years ending after December 31, 1998.
Sets a 14% alternative tax rate on corporate net capital gains, in place of the standard corporate tax on those gains.

Indexes the basis of stock and tangible business property held more than one year, increasing the purchase price by the rise in the GDP price index before computing gain or loss, so that inflation no longer counts as taxable profit.
Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers occurring after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury loses the revenue from lower capital gains rates and from estate and gift tax repeal. That shortfall must be made up through other taxes, lower spending, or larger deficits, spreading the cost across taxpayers generally, while the direct savings concentrate at the top.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The tax cuts are concentrated: capital gains are realized mainly by the highest-income households, and the estate tax applied only to the largest estates, so repeal delivers its biggest benefits to a small share of families while reducing federal revenue for everyone else.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes entirely, rather than raising the exemption, removes the tax even on the very largest fortunes, maximizing the revenue loss.

Indexing adds significant complexity: financial entities like mutual funds, REITs, and partnerships would have to track month-by-month asset ratios and valuation rules, with special carve-outs for preferred stock, net lease property, and foreign corporations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers large, permanent tax savings to the households that hold the most appreciated assets and the largest estates, while the revenue loss is spread broadly. There is a fair argument that taxing inflationary gains taxes money holders never earned, and indexing addresses that. But the combination of a 14% gains rate with full estate tax repeal — with no revenue offset in the bill — is a heavily top-weighted package whose cost falls on taxpayers as a whole.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Wayne Allard introduced the bill on February 12, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the measure three times over 1998 — February 12, May 14, and July 10 — but no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill remained pending there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing capital gains rates and the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes remained in place, and the broad taxpayer base was spared the revenue loss the bill would have caused. Heirs of large estates and holders of appreciated assets lost the tax savings they would have received.

for.name: Sen. Wayne Allard
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, delivered introductory remarks on three dates in 1998, and pressed for its consideration.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. William Roth (R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 12, 1998 and took no further action; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only recorded support was the Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, with no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.industry: Investors and heirs of large estates
industries.note: The bill cuts the capital gains rate to 14% and eliminates the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes — benefits that concentrate among the wealthiest households. The savings come at the cost of federal revenue borne by taxpayers generally.

Indexed basis and a lower gains rate apply to regulated investment companies and their shareholders, making stock investment more tax-favored. Ordinary savers hold funds through retirement accounts, though most fund gains accrue to wealthier households.

industries.industry: Estate planning, insurance, and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Full repeal of the estate and gift taxes eliminates much of the estate-planning and life-insurance business built around those taxes. Consumers lose a service market but also the tax exposure that drove it.
A 14% alternative rate on corporate capital gains lowers the tax on corporate asset sales. The benefit accrues to shareholders rather than wage earners.
